main_issue: The two cases share one coherent sanitizer-bypass mechanism, but the guideline begins with an overbroad generic source-to-sink template and does not clearly define the critical invariant: every attacker-controlled child node in a security-sensitive container must be included in sanitization or removed before the sanitized container is emitted.
suggested_guideline: When sanitizing a security-sensitive DOM container such as a STYLE element, treat all original child nodes as attacker-controlled input. Detect containers with multiple, mixed, or malformed child nodes; aggregate and sanitize every content-bearing child as appropriate for its node type, then rebuild the container from the sanitized result. Do not sanitize or replace only the first child while retaining later original children. After reconstruction, remove every obsolete original child safely, accounting for live NodeList mutation (for example, remove from the end or repeatedly remove the first remaining node). Report paths where unscanned or unremoved sibling nodes can survive sanitization and be interpreted by the browser.
evidence_notes: CVE-2022-28367: processStyleTag scans and replaces only ele.getFirstChild(); later STYLE child nodes are neither included in CssScanner input nor removed, allowing content smuggling past the sanitizer.
CVE-2022-29577: the partial fix aggregates child text for scanning, but writes cleaned CSS only to the first child; safety still depends on correctly removing every remaining original child.

Both cases concern the same source shape (attacker-controlled multiple STYLE children), sink/boundary (browser interpretation after AntiSamy sanitization), missing guard (complete child-node accounting and cleanup), and safe fix (rebuild sanitized content and remove all residual children).
